title: Liberty Bell
status_note: Not rung since the fatal crack of 1846.

place.label: Liberty Bell Center, Independence NHP, Philadelphia
place.coords_source: OpenStreetMap Nominatim lookup of the named site (ODbL)

maker: Lester & Pack, Whitechapel (1752); recast by John Pass and John Stow, Philadelphia (1753)

alloy.note: about 70% copper and 25% tin with small amounts of lead, zinc, arsenic, gold and silver (NPS info sheet)

timeline.event: Ordered for the Pennsylvania State House
Cast at Whitechapel by Thomas Lester and Thomas Pack
Has arrived in Philadelphia by this date; cracks on a test ring
Recast twice by John Pass and John Stow in Philadelphia
The Pass and Stow bell is raised in the State House steeple (early June)
NPS: no evidence the bell rang on July 4 or 8, 1776 (it did ring for the Stamp Act and its repeal)
The Anti-Slavery Record first calls it the Liberty Bell
Repaired for Washington's birthday, rung, and cracked beyond use
Travels across the country to San Francisco and back, its last trip

tiers.everyday: The Liberty Bell was made for the Pennsylvania State House (now Independence Hall). It weighs 2,080 lb and cracked for good in 1846. It became a symbol of freedom for abolitionists and many others.
tiers.student: NPS: ordered in 1751, first cast at Whitechapel (Lester & Pack) in 1752, cracked on test and recast twice by Pass and Stow in 1753. About 70% copper and 25% tin; 2,080 lb, 46.5 in across, 3 ft high. A thin crack was repaired in February 1846; it cracked again on 23 February 1846 and has not been rung since. NPS finds no evidence it rang on 4 or 8 July 1776; abolitionists named it the Liberty Bell in 1835.
